title: Article Archive: Education What Teachers Think About the 'Science of Reading'
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: A Fordham Institute/RAND survey of K-3 teachers found measurable but incomplete progress in teacher knowledge of the science of reading: only about half provide systematic phonics instruction, and knowledge gaps are worst in schools serving students in poverty. Wexler argues that most commentators have focused too narrowly on the phonics side of the science of reading, while the comprehension side — which rests on building students' background knowledge — remains poorly understood and underimplemented. The survey found 58 percent of teachers incorrectly believe reading comprehension depends on generalizable skills rather than prior knowledge, and 14 percent have little interest in knowledge-based approaches. The article also addresses the growing AI challenge in writing instruction: many teachers are requiring in-class, handwritten essays as a solution to ChatGPT use, but Wexler argues this creates new problems — less time for research, revision, and complex texts — and that the deeper fix is actually teaching writing rather than just assigning it.
points: The 'science of reading' has been narrowed in most state policies to mean phonics, leaving out the equally important (and less understood) knowledge-building dimension of reading comprehension.
Teacher knowledge is lowest in schools serving low-income students, precisely where strong reading instruction is most needed — a compounding inequity in the reform's implementation.

Pre-service teacher preparation programs are actually correlated with lower knowledge of the science of reading than on-the-job training; what teachers learn in university programs about reading is often counterproductive.

The AI-in-writing problem has led many teachers to require all writing in class by hand, but this solution sacrifices research depth, revision quality, and time — problems the author argues only get solved by teaching writing, not just assigning it.
Teaching students to create a linear outline before drafting and to construct good sentences reduces the cognitive burden of writing and may make students less likely to resort to AI shortcuts.
quotes: Alarmingly, teacher knowledge of the 'science of reading' is lowest in schools serving students who live in poverty, where 41 percent of teachers were not clearly in favor of systematic phonics instruction. Students from low-income families are generally most in need of such instruction.

Teachers who said they relied on their pre-service training for knowledge of the 'science of reading' knew less than those who had gotten training on the job — and those who said their pre-service programs emphasized the 'science of reading' knew the least.
The typical approach tries to teach comprehension skills in the abstract, even though the evidence indicates that relevant knowledge is far more important to comprehension than general 'skills.'

58 percent of teachers incorrectly said that reading comprehension depends on 'a set of generalizable skills that can be applied to most texts,' as opposed to 'what students already know about the topic and the specific vocabulary used in a text.'

If you had done this survey five or ten years ago, you almost certainly would have found fewer teachers endorsing the idea of teaching phonics or building knowledge. At the same time, the survey also reveals that a lot of teachers still aren't on board with those concepts.

One teacher quoted in the Times article, for example, tells her students, 'I want you to write out a really rough, terrible draft in your writers' notebooks. And then I want you to scratch it out and rewrite it.' That might work well for some students, but most will likely find writing easier if they've been taught how to create a linear outline before writing a draft.
